title: Japanese: Everyday Words
subtitle: 40 words and phrases for every day

cards.example: I drink a glass of water.
cards.note: mizu. The kanji shows a stream with splashes. 水曜日 (suiyōbi), Wednesday, is literally "water day".

cards.example: The fire keeps us warm in the evening.
cards.note: hi. The kanji shows a campfire with sparks. 火曜日 (kayōbi), Tuesday, is "fire day".

cards.example: The mountain is covered in snow.
cards.note: yama. Three peaks, easy to recognize. In mountain names the character is often read "san", as in 富士山 (Fujisan).

cards.example: The river flows through the city.
cards.note: kawa. Three flowing lines like running water. In names it is often pronounced "gawa", as in 品川 (Shinagawa).

cards.example: It is shady under the tree.
cards.note: ki. A tree with a trunk, branches and roots. Two trees 林 (hayashi) make a grove, three trees 森 (mori) a forest.

cards.example: The flower blooms in spring.
cards.note: hana. At the top sits the grass radical 艹. 花見 (hanami) is the picnic under blossoming cherry trees.

cards.example: The dog is sleeping on the sofa.
cards.note: inu. The kanji is 大 (big) with an extra dot, like a big dog with a pricked-up ear.

cards.example: The cat is sitting by the window.
cards.note: neko. On the left is the animal radical 犭. By the way, Japanese cats say "nyā" instead of "meow".

cards.example: I read a book in the evening.
cards.note: hon. A tree 木 with a stroke at its root means "origin". That is why it also appears in 日本 (Nihon), "origin of the sun".

cards.example: The car is parked outside the door.
cards.note: kuruma. The kanji shows a cart seen from above, with axle and wheels. In 電車 (densha, train) it is read "sha".

cards.example: The station is not far.
cards.note: eki. On the left is the horse 馬: stations used to be post stations where travelers changed horses.

cards.example: Our house has a small garden.
cards.note: ie. A pig 豕 under a roof 宀, because livestock used to live in the house. For one's own home it is often read "uchi".

cards.example: My friend is coming to visit today.
cards.note: tomodachi. 達 was originally a plural marker. Today 友達 can also mean a single friend, but never a romantic partner.

cards.example: The teacher explains the task.
cards.note: sensei. Literally "born earlier". It is used not only for teachers but also for doctors, lawyers and masters of their craft. You never use it about yourself.

cards.example: He is a student in Kyoto.
cards.note: gakusei. 学 means to learn, 生 life or person. For schoolchildren, 生徒 (seito) is more common.

cards.example: I have the day off today.
cards.note: kyō. An irregular reading you simply have to learn: on their own, the characters mean "now" and "day".

cards.example: See you tomorrow.
cards.note: ashita. 明 (bright) plus 日 (day): the next day to grow bright. More formal readings are "asu" and "myōnichi".

cards.example: I went to the movies yesterday.
cards.note: kinō. 昨 means "previous". In formal texts the same characters are read "sakujitsu".

cards.example: Do you have time tomorrow?
cards.note: jikan. 時 is the hour, 間 the space in between, the same character as in "Ma". So time is the space between the hours.

cards.example: The weather is nice today.
cards.note: tenki. Literally something like "heavenly energy". Small talk often starts with いい天気ですね (ii tenki desu ne), "nice weather, isn't it?".

cards.example: The rain will stop soon.
cards.note: ame. The kanji shows drops falling from a cloud. Careful: 飴 (ame) means candy and differs only in pitch.

cards.example: The sky is clear today.
cards.note: sora. The same character can also be read "kara", and then it means empty: 空手 (karate) is the "empty hand".

cards.example: We eat breakfast at seven.
cards.note: asagohan. 朝 means morning, ご飯 cooked rice or meal. Lunch is 昼ご飯 (hirugohan), dinner is 晩ご飯 (bangohan).

cards.example: Would you like some tea?
cards.note: ocha. The お is a polite prefix. Without anything added, お茶 in Japan usually means green tea.

cards.example: The phone is ringing again.
cards.note: denwa. 電 means electricity, 話 to speak: "electric speaking". When you answer the phone, you say もしもし (moshi moshi).

cards.example: It is nice and quiet here.
cards.note: shizuka. A な-adjective: 静かな部屋 (shizuka na heya) is a quiet room. That quiet moment is exactly what this app wants to give you.

cards.example: The park is very big.
cards.note: ōkii. The kanji 大 shows a person with arms spread wide.

cards.example: The apartment is small but cozy.
cards.note: chiisai. The kanji 小 shows something small splitting into three parts. The opposite is 大きい (ōkii).

cards.example: The hotel is quite expensive.
cards.note: takai. Means both high and expensive. The opposite depends on the meaning: 安い (yasui) is cheap, 低い (hikui) is low.

cards.example: We eat at seven o'clock.
cards.note: taberu. A ru-verb: you form the polite form by replacing る with ます, giving 食べます (tabemasu).

cards.example: I would like something to drink.
cards.note: nomu. In Japanese you also "drink" medicine, even pills: 薬を飲む (kusuri o nomu).

cards.example: Shall we go for a walk?
cards.note: iku. The destination takes the particle に or へ: 駅に行く (eki ni iku), to go to the station. Whether on foot or by train doesn't matter.

cards.example: Can you see the moon?
cards.note: miru. The kanji shows an eye 目 on two legs. The polite form is 見ます (mimasu).

cards.example: I want to rest on Sunday.
cards.note: yasumu. The kanji shows a person 亻 leaning against a tree 木. It is also where おやすみ, good night, comes from.

cards.example: Thank you for your help.
cards.note: arigatō. More polite is ありがとうございます. The word comes from 有り難い, "hard to come by", meaning something rare and precious.

cards.example: Excuse me, where is the station?
cards.note: sumimasen. You use it to apologize, to address strangers or to call a waiter. It is often a thank-you too, when someone has gone to trouble for you.

cards.example: Good morning, did you sleep well?
cards.note: ohayō. Among friends おはよう is enough; to be polite you say おはようございます. The word is related to 早い (hayai, early).

cards.example: Good evening, nice to see you.
cards.note: konbanwa. The final は is pronounced "wa" because it was originally the topic particle: "as for this evening".

cards.example: Good night and sweet dreams.
cards.note: oyasumi. Comes from 休む (yasumu, to rest). To be polite you say おやすみなさい.

cards.example: Let's eat, it smells wonderful.
cards.note: itadakimasu. Said before eating, literally something like "I humbly receive". After the meal comes ごちそうさまでした.
